issues.claim: its name changed several times before settling as South Woodford
issues.correct: George Lane (1856), South Woodford (George Lane) from 5 July 1937, South Woodford from 14 December 1947 when the Central line took over.
issues.suggested_text: The ford crossed the River Roding. The station opened in 1856 as George Lane, after the road outside. It became South Woodford in 1947, when the Central line arrived.

issues.claim: Named after Southbury Road, from an old name for the southern part of Enfield.
issues.problem: No source supports 'old name for the southern part of Enfield'. The Enfield Society says the name comes from a neighbouring field; the road was Nags Head Lane until renamed Southbury Road in 1882.
issues.correct: Southbury Road (formerly Nags Head Lane) was renamed in 1882; the name Southbury derives from a neighbouring field.
issues.suggested_head: Named after Southbury Road, which took its name from a nearby field.
issues.suggested_text: The road was called Nags Head Lane until 1882. The station opened in 1891 as Churchbury and closed in 1909. It reopened in the First World War, closed again, and came back as Southbury in 1960.

issues.claim: The station opened in 1891 as Churchbury, closed in 1909, and reopened as Southbury in 1960.
issues.problem: Implies the station was shut 1909-1960; it reopened for munitions workers 1915-1919.
issues.correct: Opened 1 Oct 1891 as Churchbury; closed to passengers 1 Oct 1909; reopened 1 Mar 1915 to 1 Jul 1919; reopened as Southbury 21 Nov 1960.
issues.suggested_text: The road was called Nags Head Lane until 1882. The station opened in 1891 as Churchbury and closed in 1909. It reopened in the First World War, closed again, and came back as Southbury in 1960.

issues.claim: The street takes its name from St James's Church, built in the 19th century for the growing town.
issues.problem: Church confirmed (first St James's built 1842, rebuilt 1902, demolished c.1960s; site now a health centre), but no source found that explicitly says the street was named after it. Checked Wikipedia (Walthamstow, station), Hidden London, Walthamstow Diary.
issues.correct: Hidden London: Walthamstow's first St James's church was built in 1842, replaced 1902, demolished about sixty years later. Street-name link plausible but not documented in sources checked. Walthamstow = 'the place of welcome' (Wilcumestowe, c.1075) is confirmed.
issues.suggested_text: The street probably takes its name from St James's Church, built in 1842 for the growing town and later pulled down. Walthamstow means the place of welcome.

issues.claim: 'Stoke Newington' means the new farm by the tree stumps.
issues.problem: Stated as certain; Wikipedia gives a different reading ('new town in the wood'), and the 'stoke' element is interpreted either as 'by the tree stumps' or 'made of logs'.
issues.correct: Newington = 'new farm/town'; the added 'Stoke' (OE stoccen) is read as 'by the tree stumps', 'made of logs' or 'in the wood'. Defoe lived on Church Street; Poe attended Manor House School c.1818 (both confirmed).
issues.suggested_head: 'Stoke Newington' probably means the new farm by the tree stumps.

issues.claim: The pub, Ye Olde Swiss Cottage, still stands near the station.
issues.problem: The pub closed (temporarily Jan 2024, permanently reported Feb 2025). The building still stands and was given Asset of Community Value status in 2025, but it is no longer a working pub. (Not checked whether it has reopened since.)
issues.correct: Inn first built 1804 as The Swiss Tavern; later Ye Olde Swiss Cottage; closed by Samuel Smith's in 2025; building protected from demolition by ACV status.
issues.suggested_text: An inn has stood on this site since 1804. The pub building, Ye Olde Swiss Cottage, still stands near the station, though it closed in 2025.

issues.claim: It was recorded in 1206 as Chipeham. The spelling changed over the centuries, probably through a misreading, until it became Sydenham.
issues.problem: Spelling and the 'misreading' explanation not confirmed. The only source found gives the 1206 form as Chipenham (matching the head, not the text), Shippenham by 1315, and attributes the ch->sh change to Norman French influence; no source found for 'misreading'. Wikipedia (Sydenham, London) only says 'originally known as Sippenham'. Also the head states Cippa without hedge; source says 'likely'.
issues.correct: First recorded 1206 as Chipenham; Shippenham by 1315; likely 'homestead or enclosure of a man called Cippa'.
issues.suggested_head: 'Sydenham' started as Chipenham, probably the homestead of a man called Cippa.
issues.suggested_text: It was recorded in 1206 as Chipenham, and as Sippenham later on. The spelling kept changing over the centuries until it became Sydenham.

issues.claim: The station opened with the Victoria line in 1968.
issues.problem: The station opened in 1840 as Tottenham on the Northern & Eastern Railway; the Victoria line arrived (and the name Tottenham Hale was adopted) on 1 September 1968.
issues.correct: Opened 15 September 1840 as Tottenham; Victoria line and renaming 1 September 1968.
issues.suggested_text: 'Hale' probably comes from an old word for a nook or corner of land. The station opened in 1840 as Tottenham, and took its present name when the Victoria line arrived in 1968.

issues.claim: 'Hale' is said to come from an old word meaning to hoist or haul: goods such as timber were unloaded from the River Lea here.
issues.problem: The hoist/haul derivation appears only on Wikipedia (uncited folk explanation). Hidden London says 'Hale' means 'the nook' (the usual Old English healh, nook/corner of land), with residents of 'the Hale' recorded from the late 13th century.
issues.suggested_text: 'Hale' probably comes from an old word for a nook or corner of land. The station opened in 1840 as Tottenham, and took its present name when the Victoria line arrived in 1968.
